t.cultural and historic ensemble of the so:
On a cold northern island in the White Sea, a monk called Savvatiy and later a priest called Zosima and a hermit called German built a monastery in the 1430s that would become one of the richest and most powerful in Russia. The Solovetsky Islands, six in all, lie about a hundred and fifty kilometres south of the Arctic Circle, and the monks turned them into a self-sufficient little kingdom, with fish ponds, mills, salt works and a harbour, and a great fortress, built in the sixteenth century with boulders the size of cars. The Cathedral of the Transfiguration, with its massive whitewashed walls and onion domes, stands at the centre of a walled compound that looks, from the water, like a medieval city. UNESCO listed the ensemble in 1992.

There is a darker chapter too. After the Revolution, the Soviet authorities turned the monastery into a prison camp, among the first of the Gulag, and in the 1920s and 1930s thousands of prisoners, intellectuals, clergy and ordinary people, were held and many died here. The monastery was returned to the Church in the 1990s, and today monks again live and pray inside the walls, and the memory of the camp is marked by crosses and memorials.

You cannot ride a bike here in the usual sense. The islands have no road link, and the only ways to reach them are the summer ferries from Kem or Belomorsk on the Karelian coast, which take a few hours, or a small plane from Arkhangelsk. The nearest places for fuel and supplies are on the mainland, and on the island you will find only a few gravel tracks and local shops. Walking and cycling are the norm, and renting a bicycle is popular.

The weather is cold and changeable, with sea fog, wind and long white nights in June, when the sun hardly sets. Winters are severe, and the sea freezes. Summer, from late June to August, is the only season for visitors. Mosquitoes can be fierce.

Belugas, the white whales, come close to the shore in summer. Travel to Russia is currently complicated for foreigners, so check conditions before you plan.
t.big zayatski island@65.0,35.7:
The strangest thing on Big Zayatsky Island is made of stones, and nobody knows for certain what it was for. Scattered over the grass and heather are about thirteen spiral labyrinths, circles of boulders laid out in coils with a single winding path to the centre, and between them stand piles of stones, perhaps graves and perhaps offerings. They are thought to be three to four thousand years old, made by the people who lived on these northern shores in the Neolithic and Bronze Age, and similar labyrinths exist around the coasts of the Baltic and Scandinavia, as well as in northern Russia. Some scholars think they were ritual places, a kind of road to the world of the dead, others that they were traps for spirits or even for fish. The island is part of the Solovetsky archipelago, and falls within the area of the World Heritage site.

The island is a small, low, windswept place in the White Sea, a few kilometres from the main island, with a lighthouse, a few buildings and a population of birds. Eider ducks and gulls nest here, and in summer the ground is covered in cloudberry and crowberry. You reach it by boat from Big Solovetsky Island, and trips run only in good weather, with a guide.

There is no riding to be done here. The islands have no road link to the mainland, and for riders the nearest fuel and supplies are on the Karelian coast, at Kem or Belomorsk, where the ferry leaves. Once on Solovetsky, you can hire a bicycle, and a few gravel tracks run between lakes and chapels.

The weather decides everything. In June and July the nights are white and the sea can be calm and silver, while storms can arrive from nowhere, stranding boats for days. Take warm clothing, windproof layers and insect repellent, as the mosquitoes can be intense. The season is short, from June to August.

Walk the spiral paths if you are permitted, and notice how a simple pattern of stones can alter the way you move. As for foreign travel to Russia, conditions are currently restrictive, and you should check before you plan.
t.aqaba marine reserve@29.4,35.0:
The Gulf of Aqaba is a narrow arm of the Red Sea, a deep trench between Jordan and Saudi Arabia on one side and Sinai on the other, and its clear water holds some of the northernmost coral reefs in the world. Jordan's marine reserve runs along a short coastal strip south of Aqaba, where the mountains of the desert drop to a thin ribbon of beach and the water goes from beige to turquoise to deep blue within a hundred metres.

Aqaba is the city that makes sense of it: nearly a hundred thousand people, Jordan's only seaport, and a free-trade zone where desert and sea meet. In 1917, Arab forces under Faisal's army and T. E. Lawrence took the Ottoman-held town from the landward side, a daring move because the Turkish guns pointed out to sea. The old fort and a few historic buildings recall that. Tala Bay, further south, is a resort development, and the coast road passes dive centres.

Getting here from the north, you ride down the Desert Highway or the more spectacular King's Highway, then drop through a long descent to a hot, low-lying coast. The Dead Sea Highway is another option. In summer, temperatures at sea level can pass forty degrees, and the wind carries the smell of salt and diesel from the port. Best seasons are spring and autumn, with winter mild and pleasantly sunny, though the odd storm can bring flash floods in the wadis.

Aqaba has plenty of petrol stations, and the road south toward the Saudi border has stations. The reefs are the draw, so bring snorkel gear or arrange a dive, since the coral near shore can be reached from the beach in places. Fish markets and restaurants in town serve grilled fish and good hummus. Remember to carry water and sun protection, and check local rules for riding and camping, since this is a sensitive border area. The ride's reward is the wide silence of the gulf at sunset.
t.wadi rum protected area@29.6,35.4:
Wadi Rum looks like the moon dressed up in rust. Great walls of sandstone and granite rise sheer from a flat desert floor of red sand, cut with canyons and carved with arches, and the whole protected area covers hundreds of square kilometres south of Jordan's King's Highway and east of the Desert Highway. The nearest sizeable town is Quweira, about twenty kilometres away, and Aqaba lies roughly an hour south.

People have lived here for thousands of years. Nabataean inscriptions and carvings are spread among the rocks, along with older petroglyphs, and the water springs, such as the one near Lawrence's Spring, made the valley a stop for caravans. T. E. Lawrence wrote of it in Seven Pillars of Wisdom, and the film that made it famous in the 1960s was shot here. Today the local Bedouin run the camps, the jeep tours and the camel rides, and they know the paths and weather better than any visitor.

For riders, the main road to the village is smooth and quick, but the desert tracks beyond are sand, and a heavy road bike is no match for them. The sensible choice is to leave the machine at the visitor centre and join a local driver or guide, perhaps for sunset when the rock goes from orange to deep red and then to purple. Wind can whip up sand, and the midday summer heat is punishing. Spring and autumn are best, winter nights are cold, and the sky at night is full of stars.

Services are basic. There is a visitor centre and an entry fee for the protected area, and camps offer meals, usually chicken, rice, vegetables and flat bread cooked in the sand. Fill the tank in Aqaba or Quweira before heading in, and carry plenty of water. Mobile signal is patchy. If you stay the night in a camp, you will sleep under a roof of stars and wake to cold air and tea.
t.marathon@24.7,-81.0:
Marathon is the middle of the Florida Keys, a flat, tropical working town strung along Key Vaca and its neighbours, and the place where the Overseas Highway pauses to take a breath before the famous long bridge. About nine thousand people live here, enough for plenty of fuel, supermarkets, diners and marine shops, and most travellers stop for coffee and a pit stop before the next stretch. The sea sits on both sides of the road, turquoise on the Gulf side and a deeper blue on the Atlantic.

The Keys road has a remarkable history. Henry Flagler built a railway down the islands in the early 1900s, a feat of engineering that carried trains over open water all the way to Key West. The 1935 Labor Day hurricane destroyed much of it, killing hundreds, and the highway that followed was built on the old railway's bridges and right-of-way. Just southwest of Marathon, the original Seven Mile Bridge, now partly a pedestrian pier, runs beside the modern one and leads to little Pigeon Key, where railway workers once lived. Riding the new bridge is a long, steady, open ride with a view that never changes and never gets dull.

Riding here is easy but not relaxed. The speed limits drop to forty-five or fifty-five in the built-up parts, enforcement is real, and tourist traffic comes in waves, with rental cars drifting between lanes and sudden stops for a pelican or a photo. The corners are nonexistent, the challenge is attention, and the wind off the water can shove a light bike sideways on the bridges. Sun is fierce, so drink water, and storms pop up in summer afternoons, flooding the road with warm rain in minutes.

Wildlife is part of the charm. Marathon has a well-known turtle hospital that rehabilitates injured sea turtles, and the shallows teem with fish, rays and the occasional manatee. Sombrero Beach is a decent place for a swim and a rest, with shade and picnic tables. The best months are winter and spring, when the air is dry and mild; summer brings heat, humidity and hurricane season, which runs through the autumn. Stay a night if you can, because the sunsets here are worth it.
t.octagon earthworks@40.1,-82.4:
Two thousand years ago, a people we now call the Hopewell built a precise geometry in the fields of Licking County, Ohio, and this is where the best of it survives. The Octagon Earthworks sits on the edge of Newark, close to Heath, a neat eight-sided enclosure with walls about a metre high, opening onto a perfect circle some three hundred metres across. No one knows what the Hopewell called it, but they certainly knew what they were doing. The alignments of the walls track the extreme points of the moon's rising over an 18.6-year cycle, and the whole thing was surveyed to a remarkable accuracy, without metal tools or writing.

The site has a quirk that surprises visitors. Part of it was used as a golf course for more than a century, with fairways and bunkers laid over the ancient banks, and the country club still holds a lease. Public access is limited to set days and hours, so check before arriving. A viewing mound and a short path give a good sense of the scale. It was recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023, together with other Hopewell sites in southern Ohio.

The ride in is a gentle country run. The roads east of Columbus pass through farm fields, woodlots and quiet small towns, with a flat to rolling surface and little traffic away from the main routes. The rolling hills near Granville, a college town with a leafy main street, are pretty in autumn. The Licking River winds around the area, and in spring the fields are bright green.

Newark has about forty-eight thousand people and Heath ten thousand, so fuel and food are right at hand. Granville, a short distance away, has older inns and a couple of bakeries that suit a slow afternoon. Mosquitoes can be fierce near the water in summer. Take your time at the site, because the peace is the point, and let the strangeness of the place settle in.
Hopewell is a name from a farm. When archaeologists first dug into the earthworks of Ohio in the nineteenth century, they found some of the finest examples on land owned by a man called Mordecai Hopewell, and the name stuck for a whole culture that flourished here between about 100 BCE and 400 CE. The people themselves had no such name, and they left no writing, so what we know comes from the soil: giant geometric enclosures, burial mounds and an astonishing range of objects.

What makes the Hopewell remarkable is the reach of their trade. Graves hold copper from the shores of Lake Superior, mica from the southern Appalachians, shells from the Gulf of Mexico, and obsidian from the Rocky Mountains, sometimes as far away as what is now Yellowstone. Craftspeople turned these into ornaments and ritual tools: a mica hand, a copper bird, a pipe carved in the shape of a beaver. Ceremonial gatherings seem to have drawn people from great distances, and the earthworks were the stages for them, more like pilgrimage centres than villages.

The collection of Ohio sites, which includes the Newark Earthworks and several around Chillicothe, was added to UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2023. The Newark group was once the biggest of all, covering several square kilometres, and only parts of it survive under streets and golf fairways. At Mound City, about eighty kilometres to the south, a cluster of low burial mounds sits in a grassy enclosure beside the Scioto River and is run by the national park service.

Riding here means the quiet roads of central Ohio, with farm fields, small woodlots, and long views over gently rolling country. Surfaces are generally good and traffic is light outside Columbus and Newark. Fuel is available in Heath and Newark, just a few kilometres away. In summer, the humidity and mosquitoes can be intense, and thunderstorms roll across the plains in the afternoon. Autumn is the most pleasant season, with mild days and golden light on the grass.
t.great circle earthworks@40.0,-82.4:
Where the Hopewell builders wanted to impress, they built big, and the Great Circle at Heath is the proof. The enclosure is a ring of earth about three hundred and sixty metres across, with walls that still rise to around four metres, inside a ditch that makes them look even taller. It is the largest circular earthwork in the Americas that survives, and standing at the entrance, you see the bank curve away into the trees on both sides. Nobody knows how many baskets of soil it took, but it must have been millions.

In the middle sits a low mound shaped like a bird, known as Eagle Mound, which seems to have been a focus for ceremony. The ditch inside the wall is a puzzle: it is on the inside, which is odd for a defensive work, and so it suggests that the purpose was not defence but a sacred space. Celebrations, burials and gatherings might have taken place within the ring, and the surrounding landscape was probably covered in open woodland and prairie.

Like the Octagon a few kilometres north, the Great Circle spent much of the last two centuries in unusual hands. It was a county fairground for a time, which explains some of the damage, and the Ohio History Connection manages it now. A path leads around and across the ring, with signs that explain its history. The grass is mowed, the paths are easy, and there are benches under old trees in the shade.

The roads here are plain but pleasant. From Heath and Newark, quiet streets lead to the site, and the countryside beyond is rolling farmland with small woods and creeks. The nearby town of Granville, about eight kilometres east, has a pretty main street and a college, and the old Welsh Hills just beyond have some curving roads in the autumn colour. Fuel and food are available in Heath, Newark and Granville, and a short stop in the park makes a satisfying quiet end to a day of riding.
t.tiya@8.4,38.6:
Tiya lies some ninety kilometres south of Addis Ababa, on the high plateau of the Great Rift's northern edge, and it holds one of the strangest open-air museums in Africa. In a field beside a village, dozens of weathered stone pillars stand in clusters, some leaning, some upright, each carved with swords, symbols and abstract figures. They are stelae, grave markers raised several centuries ago, probably between the twelfth and fourteenth, by a culture whose name has been lost. UNESCO listed the site in 1980, and a custodian will usually walk you around and explain which carvings are thought to show warriors and which show something nobody has managed to read.

The country around it is farmland, gently rolling and busy with people. Teff and enset, the false banana that feeds much of southern Ethiopia, grow in the fields, and the villages are strings of low houses with tin or thatch roofs. Eucalyptus groves grow on the ridges, and the air at this altitude, comfortably above two thousand metres, is cool and clear. Women carry water and firewood along the verges, children wave from every corner, and every so often a herd of cattle will slowly cross the road with no regard for traffic.

For a rider, this is a day that needs patience and alertness. The road south from Addis through Mojo is asphalt and generally decent, but it is shared with minibuses, heavy lorries, donkey carts, goats and pedestrians, and the driving style is confident to the point of recklessness. Overtaking on blind bends is common. Daylight riding only, and watch for potholes after the rains, which fall mostly from June to September. Mojo, the nearest sizeable town on the main road, is the place to fuel, so start with a full tank from Addis, and do not count on every small village having petrol. A stop for coffee in a roadside café is a pleasure, since Ethiopia is where coffee began, and the ceremony of roasting, grinding and brewing it can last half an hour.

Bring cash in small notes for the entrance fee and any tip to the guide, and wear a hat, because the sun is strong. The light in the early morning, with mist on the fields and the stones cold and damp, is the best time to see the pillars and imagine who set them there.
t.small mucksalma island@65.0,36.0:
Somewhere in the cold, pale waters of the White Sea, a few hours by boat from the Karelian mainland, lie the Solovetsky Islands, and Small Mucksalma is one of the smaller pieces of the group. It is not a place most riders will ever reach on a motorcycle. There are no bridges or long roads, and the islands are reached by ferry or boat in summer, and by small plane when the sea freezes. So the label here is less about asphalt than about the story, and it is a remarkable one.

The monastery that dominates the main island was founded in the fifteenth century by two monks, Savvaty and Zosima, who settled here in a landscape of lakes, pine and moss. Over the following centuries it grew into a rich and fortified community, with thick granite walls, towers and a great cathedral, and the monks built canals, mills and a causeway to the neighbouring island. That causeway, a dike made of huge boulders, links the main island with Big Mucksalma, and it is an astonishing piece of medieval engineering. UNESCO recognised the cultural and historic ensemble in 1992.

The history turned dark in the twentieth century, when the Soviet authorities converted the monastery into a prison camp, one of the earliest in the Gulag system, and a hard place of forced labour and executions. The monastery has since returned to monastic life, and the memory of the camp is part of what visitors see and feel. The islands are also a natural reserve, with white nights in early summer, when the sun skims the horizon and the sea looks like polished metal, and with birds, seals and white beluga whales in the surrounding waters.

For anyone planning a ride, the honest advice is to treat this point as the far edge of a map, a reminder of the northern reaches of Europe rather than a stop on a normal route. The nearest mainland access is by boat from towns on the White Sea coast, and conditions, permits and travel advice change, so check current information before building any plan around it. In summer the weather is cool and damp, with fog and mosquitoes, and in winter, it is harsh.
t.solovetsky island@65.1,35.7:
You do not ride to Solovetsky so much as you get yourself and a bike onto a boat. The archipelago sits in the White Sea, on the southern edge of the Arctic, and the ferry or the small plane from the mainland near Kem is the only way out. Once there, the island is roughly twenty-five kilometres long and has a network of gravel and dirt tracks that make it a quiet adventure ride rather than a road trip. Allow for rain, for wind off the water, and for very long summer light around midsummer when the nights hardly darken.

The reason people make the effort is the monastery. Two monks, Savvaty and Zosima, founded a hermitage here in the fifteenth century, and it grew into one of the richest and most heavily fortified religious houses in Russia, with walls of huge granite boulders that you can see from the sea long before you land. In the 1920s the Soviets turned the whole thing into a camp, one of the first of the Gulag system, and thousands of prisoners died here. Both histories sit on the same ground and nobody on the island pretends otherwise. The monastery has been returned to the church and is again lived in, which gives the place an odd weight, tender and grim at once.

Beyond the walls the island is mostly lakes, spruce and pine forest and low hills, linked by canals the monks dug long before engines existed. There is a botanical garden planted by the monks that has no business surviving this far north, and the coast has white beluga whales in summer, if you are lucky with the boat trips. Small Mucksalma Island is reached by a causeway of stones roughly a kilometre long, built by monks, and it is an easy ride or walk across the shallows, with seabirds and a view back to the monastery.

Practical matters are thin. The island has a settlement with shops and a couple of places to eat, but supplies come by boat, so fill the tank on the mainland and bring what you cannot do without. Tracks turn to mud in rain, mosquitoes are fierce in July, and the realistic season is June to early September. Check current rules for travel to Russia before planning anything.
t.alula@26.6,37.9:
AlUla lies in a broad sandstone basin in north-west Saudi Arabia, and the first thing you notice when you arrive is the shape of the rock. Cliffs of red and ochre stand straight up from a flat valley floor, carved by wind into mushrooms, arches and buttresses, and the oasis of date palms at their base looks almost unreal against the stone. The town is around thirty thousand people, with the old mudbrick quarter still standing on the hillside above the modern streets.

Human history here is deep. The Dadanite and Lihyanite kingdoms controlled the trade in incense and spices centuries before the Nabataeans, the people of Petra, took over the oasis. At Hegra, a short ride north, more than a hundred rock-cut tombs from the first century line the sandstone outcrops, with carved facades and Nabataean inscriptions, and it was the first place in Saudi Arabia to be listed by UNESCO. Later came the Hejaz railway, built by the Ottomans to carry pilgrims, whose station buildings still stand in the desert nearby.

The riding is the real treat. Roads in the area are smooth and quiet, with fine surface, long clean sweeps across the desert plain and then a few tight turns where the highway cuts through the cliffs. Elephant Rock, a free-standing sandstone mass near the road, is the famous photo stop, best at sunset when the light turns it orange. Wind can blow sand across the road, so slow down when you see dust, and keep a close eye on sheep or camels near the verge.

Timing matters. From November to March days are warm and nights cool, ideal for riding, while from May to September temperatures reach the forties and the sun is relentless. Drink more water than you think you need, wear light long sleeves, and carry spare. Fuel and food are plentiful in AlUla itself, but distances between towns in the desert are long, so fill up before leaving. A guided visit is required for the main areas of Hegra, so book ahead.
t.bahia honda@24.7,-81.3:
Bahia Honda means deep bay, and the name is a clue to what makes this island special. Most of the Florida Keys are flat, fringed with mangroves and shallow, but here the water is deep enough close to shore that Henry Flagler's railway engineers had to build a long steel truss bridge to cross the channel. That bridge, completed in 1912 as part of the Overseas Railroad, carried trains to Key West until a hurricane in 1935 destroyed much of the line. The railroad's bridges were then converted for road traffic, and the old steel structure at Bahia Honda, with its girders overhead, was used by cars until the 1970s. Part of it now stands unused as a lookout, cut short in places, a rusty ghost above the water.

The state park here has some of the best beaches in the Keys, with pale sand, clear water and tropical vegetation. The sea is the colour of turquoise, and you can walk in warm, shallow water for a long way. Snorkelling off the beach is good, and the park is a refuge for plants and birds found nowhere else in Florida. In the evening, the sunsets over the Gulf are glorious. The park charges an entry fee, and motorcycles pay a small amount.

The Overseas Highway, US 1, runs for 113 miles from Key Largo to Key West, over dozens of islands and forty-odd bridges, and it is one of the world's great road trips. The riding is easy rather than technical, with flat, straight roads and the sea on both sides. Speed limits are strictly enforced, and the traffic can be heavy, especially on weekends and holidays. Watch for the tiny Key deer, an endangered subspecies found on Big Pine Key, close to here, and obey the lower limits at night.

Fuel is available at Big Pine Key and Marathon, and again at many places on the route, though prices are higher than on the mainland. Heat and humidity are fierce in summer, and afternoon thunderstorms arrive fast. Winter is the best season, when the air is warm and dry. Take sunscreen, water and a light rain jacket, and make time to swim.
t.erie pennsylvania@42.1,-80.1:
Erie's best feature is a sandy hook of land that curls out into Lake Erie. Presque Isle, a state park on a peninsula about seven miles long, shelters the bay and holds sandy beaches, dunes, marshes and woodland, which draw birds migrating along the lake in spring and autumn. On a summer weekend, the beaches fill with swimmers, and in winter the lake freezes into odd heaps of ice. The bay behind the peninsula was the base from which Oliver Hazard Perry built a fleet in 1813 and sailed out to defeat the British in the Battle of Lake Erie, one of the key naval victories of the War of 1812. The brig Niagara, his second flagship, has been rebuilt and is sometimes moored in the harbour.

The city itself is an industrial one, with a past in steel, paper and locomotive building, and about a hundred thousand people. It has the plain, practical look of a Great Lakes port, with brick factories, old churches and wide avenues, and downtown has a lively waterfront and a few good breweries. Lake-effect snow is a famous feature of the climate, and in some winters the city is buried under several feet in a week.

The Seaway Trail, the scenic route that follows the shores of Lake Erie, the Niagara River, Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence River, begins here in Pennsylvania. It runs northeast through vineyards, an unexpected landscape of long straight rows of grapevines between the road and the lake, thanks to a cool microclimate along the shore. Roads are flat and easy, with gentle bends, farm stands, and old farmhouses. In September, the grape harvest perfumes the air. Winds off the lake can be strong, and summer storms can arrive quickly.

Fuel and food are easy to find in Erie. For a lakeside break, there are plenty of places along the bay, and the peninsula has cafes during the season. The best time to ride is late May to early October, and the light in September is particularly good. Traffic is manageable outside the city, with the heaviest flows on summer weekends near the beaches.
t.teriberka@69.2,35.1:
Teriberka had the misfortune of being filmed beautifully. In 2014, Andrey Zvyagintsev made Leviathan here, a bleak drama about a man and the local authorities, shot against the rusting hulks and grey surf of this Barents Sea village, and the film turned an obscure fishing settlement at the end of a long road into a destination. It had been a place of Pomors and Sami for centuries, then a Soviet fishing collective that employed thousands, and then a ghost of itself when the fish processing collapsed after 1991. Its population is a little over a thousand now, though in summer it fills with visitors.

The ride up from Murmansk is the real draw. The road covers about a hundred and twenty kilometres through tundra, over a barren plateau of low hills, lakes and boulders, where the trees stop and reindeer wander. It has been rebuilt in recent years, and the tarmac is generally good, though frost heave and patches appear. Weather is violent: fog, sleet and strong winds can come in at any time of the year, and a calm blue morning can turn to white-out within an hour. In winter, the road can be closed by snow and drifts, and driving is a serious undertaking.

Teriberka itself sits where a river meets the sea, with colourful wooden houses, a few modern hotels, and boats pulled up on the shore. In winter, the Northern Lights can be seen on clear nights, and in summer, midnight sun makes the evening endless.

Fuel is the thing to plan carefully. There may be a station or two in the village, but the reliable supply is in Murmansk, so fill up before you set out and think about your range for the round trip. Cell coverage is intermittent. The nearest sizeable town is Kola, near Murmansk, and in an emergency you may be some distance from help.

The Barents Sea is the edge of the Arctic Ocean, and the water is dark, cold and powerful. Stand by it for a moment, and notice how big the sky is.
t.teriberka coast@69.2,35.1:
Just beyond the village, the coast turns into something stranger and wilder. The most famous spot is the beach known as Yarovoye, or the Dragon's Eggs, where waves have polished the stones into big, smooth, rounded shapes that lie scattered across the shingle like the nests of some sea monster. Further along, a small waterfall drops straight off a cliff into the sea, a rarity anywhere in the world.

The geology is old. This is part of the Baltic Shield, among the oldest rocks on earth, scraped by ice and worn by water, and in the low light of the north it takes on a purple and gold tone. The vegetation is tundra, with dwarf birch, crowberry, mosses and lichens, and in autumn the ground turns red and bronze. Seabirds nest on the cliffs, including kittiwakes and guillemots, and with luck you can spot seals offshore. Whales sometimes pass at a distance.

Expect gravel, sand and rock, with sudden puddles and soft patches after rain, and be prepared to turn back if conditions look bad. Wind is relentless, and the sea can throw spray over the lower parts. Fog rolls in without warning, and distances are hard to judge. Respect the cliffs. The edges are unstable, and waves can be larger than they look.

Seasons shape everything. Summer, from late June to August, gives midnight sun and mild weather, with temperatures around ten to fifteen degrees, and mosquitoes inland. September brings the first aurora, and crisp, colourful tundra. Winter is dark, with deep snow, extreme cold and wind, and the road is a serious expedition.

For fuel, carry enough from Murmansk, since the village has little. A flask of tea and something to eat is a good idea, because the wind chills you quickly. Cafés in Teriberka, about a kilometre and a bit away, can warm you up afterward. Come in the evening, when the low sun lights the stones, and the sea is the colour of slate.
t.varzuga@66.4,36.6:
Varzuga is a village at the end of a long, rough road, on the Tersky coast of the Kola Peninsula, where the Varzuga River runs into the White Sea. It has been a Pomor settlement since at least the fifteenth century, and the name appears in old Novgorod records, which makes it one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the north. The people lived by fishing, salmon above all, salt-making and sea trade, and the houses are big, tall wooden buildings with carved trim, built to survive long winters.

The great sight here is the Dormition Church, a wooden tent-roofed church built in 1674, which stands on a low rise above the river and is among the best examples of northern timber architecture. Its slender tower, silver with age, rises above the village against a wide sky, and the interior has a plain beauty. Nearby are an old wooden belfry and other buildings from the Pomor era.

The Varzuga is also one of the great Atlantic salmon rivers of Russia, with a fishery that attracts anglers from around the world, mainly from June to September. The river is wide and clear, running through forest and tundra, and the lower stretches are a tidal estuary with sandbanks and birds. Seals are sometimes seen near the mouth. The White Sea coast has long summer light, with evenings that never get dark in June.

The road to Varzuga is part of the adventure. Traffic is minimal, so a breakdown can mean a long wait, and mobile coverage is poor. Mosquitoes and midges are ferocious in July, and a head net is a good idea. The best time is probably late June to August, with the earliest and latest weeks being cooler and quieter.

Fuel is a serious issue. Bring food and water as well, since village shops are small. Spend the evening listening to the river and watching the light on the church. It is a very quiet place.
t.lovozero@68.0,35.0:

t.paratunka@53.0,158.2:

t.vilyuchinsky pass@52.7,158.2:

Other volcanoes appear in the distance when the weather clears, including Avachinsky and Koryaksky across the bay, and the light at dusk makes them glow. It is a lonely place and a humbling one, which is exactly why riders come.
t.khalaktyrsky beach@53.0,158.9:
Khalaktyrsky Beach is a strip of black volcanic sand on the Pacific coast of Kamchatka, about fifteen kilometres from the regional capital, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky. The sand is dark and fine, made of crushed lava, and it runs for kilometres along the shore with the surf rolling in from a cold, grey ocean. Behind it rises the long skyline of the Kamchatka volcanoes, including the cone of Avachinsky, which on a clear day gives the beach one of the most dramatic backdrops in the world.

The surface is a mix of asphalt and gravel, and the last stretch to the sand can be rough and potholed. In clear weather you may see a thin plume rising from a distant volcano, a reminder that this is an active landscape. Walk along the tide line, feel the heavy, warm sand beneath your boots, and let the waves do their work. It is a good place to end a day.
t.ust bolsheretsk@52.8,156.3:

t.seven mile bridge@24.7,-81.2:

t.dodola@7.0,39.2:

t.dinsho@7.1,39.8:

t.sanetti plateau@6.9,39.7:

t.elephant rock@26.7,38.0:

t.hegra@26.8,38.0:

AlUla town, about twenty kilometres away, has fuel and food, and it is the place to fill the tank and carry water. Bring a hat, sunglasses and patience; the heritage here rewards slow looking.
t.harrat uwayrid viewpoint@26.6,37.9:

t.kimberley@44.4,-80.5:

Fuel is another matter. Eugenia has none, and Markdale, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest town with services, though it is small, so check your gauge. Flesherton, a little to the north-east, is another place to try. Collingwood and Meaford are much larger and further. Bring some food or plan to eat in Markdale or Flesherton, because the village has little beyond the falls. October brings colour, but spring, with the water high and the woods still bare, is just as good for the falls themselves.
t.addis ababa@9.0,38.7:
At about 2,350 metres, Addis Ababa is one of the highest capitals on Earth, and you feel it in the first hour: the sun is strong, the air is thin and cool, and a flight of stairs is a small event. The city sits in a bowl of eucalyptus-covered hills, founded in the 1880s by Emperor Menelik II and his wife Taytu, whose name for it, the new flower, stuck. It is a sprawling, restless, cheerful place, and the pace of building is astonishing.

Traffic is the main thing to understand. Blue minibus taxis stop wherever they like, pedestrians cross in streams, goats and donkeys appear, and lane markings are advisory. Ride defensively, keep your distance and use the horn like a language. The Ring Road is quicker but tough, and the new light rail and expressways are changing the map every year. The rainy season runs roughly from June to September, with heavy afternoon downpours that turn gutters into streams, while October to February is dry, bright and ideal.

Do not miss the National Museum, which holds the skeleton of Lucy, the famous 3.2-million-year-old hominin found in the Afar region in 1974, known locally as Dinkinesh, meaning you are marvellous. The Merkato, said to be among the largest open-air markets in Africa, is a maze to enter only with a guide. Then take the road up Entoto, the hill behind the city, where eucalyptus smoke hangs in the air and women carry impossible loads of firewood down the slopes, and where the old churches and the view over the city repay the climb.

Fuel is available throughout the city, but outside it, queues and shortages can occur, so fill up whenever you can. Coffee is a point of pride, since the plant is native to Ethiopia, and a traditional ceremony, with the beans roasted in front of you and served in three rounds, is an hour well spent. Pair it with injera and a plate of tibs, and the ride that begins here is already worth it.
t.anzer island@65.1,36.1:
Anzer is the second-largest of the Solovetsky Islands, a small archipelago in the White Sea that has played an outsized role in Russian history. A monastery was founded on the main island in the fifteenth century, and it grew into a fortress, wealthy and powerful, with granite walls whose boulders were moved by hand. On Anzer, the monks established a hermitage, or skete, which sits on a hill: a landscape of pine, spruce, small lakes and cold sea that looks very much like Finland's coasts.

The twentieth century added a darker chapter. In the 1920s the Soviet authorities turned the monastery into a prison camp, the first of the Gulag complex, and thousands of people were held on these islands under harsh conditions. Today the monastery has been restored and is open to pilgrims, and the islands are a UNESCO World Heritage site, combining the sacred and the tragic, so a quiet and respectful manner suits the place.

For riders, the practical point is that you do not arrive by bike. The islands are reached by boat from the mainland, from the port of Kem or from Belomorsk, and the crossing takes a few hours, depending on the weather. The White Sea can be rough, with fog and cold wind, and the season is short, with the main window from June to August. In the white nights of early summer, the sun barely sets, and the light on the water is extraordinary.

Leave the bike on the mainland and plan the Karelian roads that lead to the ferry with care. They are long, straight and lonely, running through forest and bog, with few villages, so take fuel whenever you see it, and carry water and food. On the island itself, small tracks and footpaths link the churches and lakes, and bicycles are often rented. Mosquitoes in July are fierce, and a net is a wise purchase. It is the kind of place that stays with you.
t.petropavlovsk kamchatsky@53.0,158.7:
Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky sits on Avacha Bay, one of the finest natural harbours in the world, at the southeastern end of the Kamchatka Peninsula, and it feels like the edge of everything. There is no road from here to the rest of Russia, so the city is reached by air or sea, and the peninsula around it holds more volcanoes than towns. The town was founded in 1740 by the expedition of Vitus Bering, and named after his two ships, the St Peter and the St Paul. It was a naval base throughout the Soviet era and closed to foreigners for decades.

The skyline is dominated by volcanoes. Koryaksky, a symmetrical cone of about 3,450 metres, and Avachinsky, about 2,750 metres, stand to the north of the city, snow-capped for much of the year, and Avachinsky is active, with a plume of steam on some days. On a clear day, they glow pink in the morning light, a sight that is part of the city's identity. The harbour holds fishing boats and naval vessels, with a monument to Bering on the waterfront. Salmon runs, brown bears and sea eagles are part of the surroundings, and the region's Pacific coast is wild and little visited.

The roads outside town are few but spectacular. The road toward Vilyuchinsk, a naval submarine base across the bay, and the Vilyuchinsky volcano, crosses a pass with views over the bay, while the road to the Khalaktyrsky beach leads to a long, dark strand of volcanic sand facing the Pacific. The surface varies from good tarmac to rough gravel, and rain, fog and wind can come quickly. Bears are a real concern, and you should make noise on walks and never leave food around. The riding season is short, usually from June to September, with snow possible at higher altitude outside that period.

Petropavlovsk is a city of nearly two hundred thousand, with fuel stations, shops, repair services and hotels. Yelizovo, about twenty-five kilometres north, has the airport and more services. Beyond, stations are scarce, so fill the tank and carry spares if you plan to go far. Mobile signal may fade away from the city.

Seafood is the thing to eat here, king crab, salmon and red caviar, and prices are lower than you might expect. The hot springs in the hills are a fine reward after a day in the cold.
t.balchit@8.8,38.6:
Southwest of Addis Ababa the high plateau starts to roll, and the names on the map begin to belong to farms and villages rather than to cities. Balchit is one of those names, a small place in the Oromia highlands beyond Sebeta, and I will be straight with you that it is not a destination in its own right. What it offers is a sample of the country that surrounds the capital: red-brown fields, eucalyptus groves, round huts and squared houses with tin roofs, and a sky of enormous size at around two thousand metres above the sea.

Addis Ababa itself stands at roughly 2,350 metres, among the highest capitals in the world, and the thin air has a real effect on a motorcycle's power and on a rider's stamina. The plateau is farmed intensively, with teff, the tiny grain from which the sour pancake injera is made, wheat, barley and beans, and in the wet season from June to September the whole region goes bright green. Rain falls heavily in those months, often in the afternoon, so mornings are the best time to ride. The dry season, from October to February, is clearer, with cool nights and clean sunlit days.

The road west from the capital toward Sebeta and beyond is a main route, busy with trucks, minibuses, donkeys, goats and pedestrians, and driving habits are unpredictable. Surfaces on main roads are mostly paved but can be broken, and on side roads they turn to dirt, which becomes slippery when wet. Ride defensively, avoid the dark, and expect that livestock will appear without warning. The people of the villages are usually curious and friendly, and a greeting in Amharic or Oromo is met with delight.

Fuel is available in Sebeta, a town of about twenty thousand people some eighteen kilometres away, and in Addis Ababa, further along. Do not count on stations in the smaller places, and fill your tank whenever you can. Ethiopian coffee, served in the traditional ceremony with roasted beans and incense, is offered in many villages, and taking a cup is both polite and delicious. The smell of woodsmoke and eucalyptus, which drifts over the hills in the evening, is the smell of the highlands.
t.atebella@8.7,38.6:
Atebella lies among the farmlands that stretch south-west of Sebeta, and what there is to say about it is really a description of the countryside. The plateau here is a patchwork of small plots, divided by hedges of cactus and euphorbia, and dotted with trees whose silhouettes look like umbrellas. It is a landscape shaped by generations of smallholders, and in the early morning, with the sun low and the mist lying in the hollows, it looks as though it has hardly changed in a century. Cattle with long horns are driven along the road by boys with sticks.

One of the most visible features of the highlands is the eucalyptus. It is not native; the trees were brought from Australia in the late nineteenth century at the time of Emperor Menelik II, who moved his capital to the site of Addis Ababa and found that the surrounding hills had been stripped of firewood. The fast-growing eucalyptus solved the problem, and now it is everywhere, in tall stands that scent the air with menthol. They are also used to build scaffolding, a surprising sight in the city, where scaffold poles are often bundles of eucalyptus lashed with rope.

The roads here are a test of concentration. Even the paved ones are shared by carts, minibuses and pedestrians, and drivers use their horns constantly. Pace yourself, and treat each blind corner as if a donkey might be waiting behind it. On the gravel tracks, a good eye for the surface is essential, especially after rain, when the red clay becomes treacherous. Altitude will reduce power, and a light bike may suffer more than a heavy one. It is cooler than you might expect for a country so near the equator, with temperatures in the teens and twenties during the day, and cold at night.

Sebeta, about twenty kilometres away, is the nearest town for fuel and supplies, and Addis Ababa lies beyond. Take water, a spare tube if you have a small bike, and a little cash in small notes. Cafes in villages serve tea with sugar, bread and sometimes a bowl of shiro, a thick chickpea stew eaten with injera. The evenings come quickly, around six, and the sunsets over the plateau are red and gold. It is a place to look and listen, and a reminder that most of the world lives in places like this.
t.kella@8.7,38.6:
Kella is another small name on the plateau south-west of the capital, and its interest lies in what you pass on the way. The old road leads out of Addis Ababa through Sebeta, a town that grew around a railway and market, and beyond it climbs gently into high farmland, with slopes of green and tan, groves of eucalyptus and, in the distance, the shape of the mountains that rim the Rift. At this latitude and height the sun is strong, but the air is cool, and the clarity of the light is memorable.

Many of the villages in this region have a church or two, often round, with a thatched or tin roof and painted walls inside, belonging to the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, one of the oldest Christian churches in the world. On Sundays and saints' days the paths fill with worshippers dressed in white, with white cotton shawls called netela, and the sound of chanting and drumming drifts across the fields. If you encounter such a gathering, slow down, keep your distance and be respectful; photographing people at worship without permission is not appreciated.

The riding is a contrast of terrain. The tarmac sections are usually decent, with long, easy curves over rolling hills, while side roads turn to dirt and stones. Rain, from June to September, can wash out sections of track and make steep descents hazardous. Early morning is the best time, with light traffic and lovely visibility. The locals will often wave, and children may run beside the bike calling out, a friendly custom that is easy to enjoy but needs care because they can dart into the road.

There are few services here. The nearest town of any size is Sebeta, with Addis Ababa farther along, and fuel is scarce on the rural roads, so plan carefully and fill the tank before you leave. A small shop may sell bottled water, biscuits and soft drinks. You will smell woodsmoke, damp earth and the sweet, peppery aroma of roasting coffee, a scent that tells you you are in the country where coffee began. Take a moment to enjoy the sheer scale of the landscape, with the ridges stacking up into the haze.
t.big mucksalma island@65.0,36.0:
Bolshaya Muksalma is a low, quiet island in the White Sea, part of the Solovetsky archipelago, and it is not a place you reach by motorway. The islands lie in the cold, shallow water of Onega Bay, and getting there takes a boat or a small plane in the short summer season, so anyone thinking about this point as a motorcycle stop should first work out the logistics of crossing the water with a vehicle. The island itself is flat, with grassy meadows, small pine woods and a rocky shore, and a long stone causeway built by the monks connects it to the main island, Great Solovetsky.

The history of the archipelago is dramatic. In the fifteenth century two monks, Savvaty and German, followed by Zosima, settled on the main island and founded what became the great Solovetsky Monastery, which grew into one of the wealthiest and most powerful religious houses in Russia, with a massive fortress wall of boulders. The monks were farmers and engineers, and they dug canals, built mills and managed farms and pastures across the islands, and Muksalma was part of that system. In the twentieth century the monastery was turned into one of the first camps of the Soviet prison system, and thousands of prisoners died there. UNESCO listed the cultural and historic ensemble of the islands in 1992.

The nature is remarkable too. The White Sea is home to beluga whales, which come to the shallows near the islands in summer, and seals haul out on the rocks. Birds are abundant, with eiders, terns and gulls nesting on the shores, and the forest has mushrooms and berries in late summer. Nearby, on Big Zayatsky Island, are mysterious spiral stone labyrinths laid out thousands of years ago, whose purpose is unknown. Summer nights are pale and light, since the islands lie just below the Arctic Circle, and the air smells of wet moss, pine and salt.

Weather can change quickly, with fog and cold winds, and the sea can be rough. Bring layers, waterproofs and insect repellent, since mosquitoes can be fierce in July. This is a place for quiet and slow exploration, not for speed, and it asks for patience in return.
t.small zayatsky@65.0,35.7:
This point lies in the White Sea, off the coast of Karelia, and no road leads to it. Small Zayatsky belongs to the little Zayatsky islands in the Solovetsky archipelago, which sits some sixty kilometres out from the mainland, and getting there means a boat. The name comes from the Russian word for hare, and the islands are low, windswept and covered with moss, crowberry, juniper and stunted pine. On a clear day in summer the water is pale and cold, the light is long, and the white nights of June make it hard to know when evening begins.

The islands are known for something far older than the monastery that dominates the archipelago. On the larger of the two, the Bolshoi Zayatsky, archaeologists have recorded more than a dozen stone labyrinths, spirals of boulders laid out on the ground, along with burial cairns and stone settings thought to be about three to four thousand years old. Nobody knows for certain what they were for; theories include ritual paths, fish traps, or maps of the afterlife, and local Pomors later gave them names. Walking around the stone spirals is a strange experience, since the pattern is clear only when you stand within it.

The nearby main island has a very different history. The Solovetsky Monastery, founded in the fifteenth century, grew into a fortress and a centre of the White Sea trade, and then in the twentieth century the Soviet state used it as the first and one of the most notorious camps of the Gulag. The story hangs over the island, and the monastery has been returned to the church and rebuilt. The island is a World Heritage site.

For a rider, the realistic version of this ride is on the main Solovetsky island, which has a few gravel and dirt roads, crossed by lakes and canals dug by the monks, and on the Karelian mainland, where the roads to Kem and Belomorsk run through forest and bog. Ferries and boats to the islands run only in the warmer months, and the sea can be rough, so crossings are cancelled in bad weather. Mosquitoes in summer are ferocious, and the best defence is a headnet and patience. Current rules for foreign visitors in Russia and on the archipelago should be checked well in advance.
t.key west@24.6,-81.8:
Mile Marker 0 is a small thing to stand beside, a green sign at the corner of Whitehead and Fleming streets, but after about a hundred and thirty miles of bridges and causeways over water the colour of a swimming pool, it feels like a finish line in the most literal sense. Key West is the end of US 1, and the end of the road in the continental United States, closer to Havana than to Miami's downtown skyscrapers by a surprisingly small margin.

The road that got you here is the story. Henry Flagler, the oil magnate, built a railway across the keys that reached the island in 1912, a stunning gamble that was called Flagler's Folly until it worked. Then the Labor Day hurricane of 1935 flattened parts of it, killing hundreds, and the bankrupt railway sold its right of way to the state. The highway you ride today uses much of those old bridges and embankments, including the famous Seven Mile Bridge, which gives the sensation of floating over shallow, bright green and turquoise flats with nothing on either side but sky and sea.

Key West itself is a small, flat island of old wooden conch houses with louvred shutters and tin roofs, tropical gardens and free-ranging chickens that wander across the road with perfect confidence. Ernest Hemingway lived here in the 1930s, and his house, now a museum, is home to a colony of polydactyl cats. The evening ritual is the sunset gathering at Mallory Square, with street performers, vendors and a cheering crowd, and Duval Street, the long main drag, is loud, silly and exactly what its reputation promises. Quieter streets a block or two away are far nicer to walk.

Riding in town is slow by necessity. Streets are narrow, scooters and bicycles weave everywhere, and parking is a puzzle, so a motorcycle is a real advantage. Fuel is on the island, and prices are higher than on the mainland. Food is built on seafood, with conch fritters, fresh fish sandwiches and key lime pie, which locals argue about, including whether it should be green. Spend a little time at the southernmost point marker, an oversized buoy with an eternal queue for photographs.

The heat and humidity are heavy from May to October, with afternoon storms, and hurricane season runs June to November. Winter is the comfortable season, with warm days and cooler evenings, though it is also the busiest and priciest time.
t.havana@23.1,-82.4:
Havana comes at you all at once: sea wind, car horns, ocean spray over the Malecón, pastel colonnades in various stages of collapse, and the unmistakable smell of old engines and the sea. It is the capital of Cuba and home to roughly two million people, and the old centre, La Habana Vieja, was given UNESCO World Heritage status in 1982 for its Spanish colonial streets and fortifications.

As a starting point it is something of a challenge, because the city is big and the road surfaces are rough. Potholes, missing manhole covers, slow bicycles, horse carts, and old American cars and Soviet-era trucks all share the same road, and nobody is in a hurry. Ride as if everyone around you might do something unexpected, because they will, and avoid riding after dark if you can. The famous seafront promenade is best for a slow, windswept cruise at sunset, with the sun going down behind the city.

The history is everywhere, from the Spanish forts that guarded the harbour to the revolutionary monuments and the grand, faded mansions of the pre-revolution elite. Havana has been a stopover for treasure fleets, a pleasure ground, and a city under embargo for decades, and the tension between those stories shows in its buildings. Music leaks from open doors, and old men play dominoes on every corner.

The thing to know about riding in Cuba is that fuel is a recurring problem. Supplies can be unpredictable, queues form without warning, and stations in the countryside may have nothing at all. Fill up whenever you see a working pump, ask locally about the next one, and be sensible about distances. Start early, because the road west is long, and give yourself time for the unexpected. The reward is a green, open island that opens up quickly once you leave the capital.
t.vinales valley@22.6,-83.7:
The Viñales Valley is one of those places where the landscape looks like a stage set. Flat red fields lie between steep, rounded limestone hills called mogotes, sheer-sided and covered in vegetation, standing like green loaves on a tablecloth. They are the remains of an ancient cave system whose roof collapsed over millions of years, and the surrounding karst is among the oldest in the Caribbean. The valley sits in the western province of Pinar del Río, and UNESCO recognised it as a cultural landscape in 1999.

What makes it cultural, not merely beautiful, is the way people still farm. This is Cuba's tobacco country, and the red earth is planted with the leaf that goes into the island's cigars, grown in small plots and often ploughed with oxen. Farmers dry their harvest in thatched barns, and visitors are often invited in to see how it is done and to taste the result. Coffee, beans and maize grow in between, and the little town of Viñales itself, about a kilometre away, is a street of low, colourful houses with deep porches.

Getting here means a long ride west from Havana, first on the broad, often empty national motorway and then on the older roads through Pinar del Río. The surfaces vary from good to bad without warning, and you should watch for potholes, animals, bicycles and horse-drawn carts, especially near villages. The valley road itself is gently winding, with views opening onto the mogotes at nearly every bend, and the best light is in the early morning, when mist hangs low between the hills, and again in the late afternoon.

Viñales has places to eat and drink, many of them in family homes, and the food is simple, hearty and plentiful. Pinar del Río, about twenty kilometres away, is the larger town. Fuel in Cuba is unpredictable, so fill up whenever you can and do not count on a station being open. Leave time to turn off the engine and just sit; the valley rewards stillness.
t.aqaba@29.5,35.0:
Aqaba is the end of the line, and the reward is the sea. Jordan has just a few dozen kilometres of coastline, all of it on the Gulf of Aqaba at the top of the Red Sea, and this is where it is. After a long day crossing the desert from Amman, either on the fast Desert Highway or the lower, rift-valley road along the Dead Sea and Wadi Araba, you arrive in a town of about ninety-five thousand people where the water is turquoise and the hills behind it are the colour of rust.

The road in is part of the ride's character. The Dead Sea Highway drops to the lowest land on Earth, then follows the rift valley south with Israel and the Negev on the far side of the border and the mountains of Edom rising on your left, a dry, huge landscape with little shade. Winds can be strong, heat in summer can top forty degrees, and distances between fuel stops are real, so top up whenever you pass a station. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; winter is mild and comfortable.

Aqaba has a long memory. The ancient city of Ayla lay here, a trading port for Nabataeans and Romans and later an early Islamic town, and in 1917 it was captured by Arab forces from the landward side, in a surprise attack on the Ottoman garrison led by Faisal's army with T. E. Lawrence, which is why the Arab Revolt flag flies above the town on one of the tallest flagpoles in the world. The fort at the harbour is small but pleasant, and the old streets of the town have fish restaurants and sweet shops to match.

For a rider, Aqaba is practical. There is fuel, food and hotels, and the evenings are cool enough to sit outside by the water. The coral reef just off the beach is among the best in the region, and snorkelling after a hot day on the road is the best possible way to end the ride. A duty-free zone means the shopping is cheap and the town is relaxed.
t.milkovo@54.7,158.6:
Milkovo is the quiet crossroads of central Kamchatka, a village of around eight thousand people on the Kamchatka River, where the long road from the capital, Petropavlovsk, forks toward the hot-spring country of Esso and toward the great volcano group around Klyuchi. There is no grand sight in the village itself. It exists because someone has to sell fuel, bread and tinned fish to everyone passing, and because the broad river valley is flat enough to farm.

The riding here is of the open, high-latitude kind. The central road runs north through long straights, birch and larch woods, boggy clearings and low rolling hills, with snow-topped volcanoes appearing now and then on the horizon like rumours. The tarmac can be good for stretches and then break up into frost-heaved patches, and distances between settlements are large, so top up whenever you pass a pump. The season is short. Summer, roughly late June to early September, brings long daylight, mosquitoes, and bear-watching opportunities, and by October the first snow is already on the ground. Bad weather can arrive quickly from the Pacific or the Sea of Okhotsk.

Kamchatka is a Ring of Fire peninsula, and the volcanic nature of the land shapes everything. The Klyuchevskaya group to the north includes Klyuchevskaya Sopka, at around 4,750 metres the tallest active volcano in Eurasia, often wearing a plume of steam. Hot springs bubble from the ground in many valleys, and the soil is dark with volcanic ash. The Kamchatka River itself is one of the great salmon rivers of the Pacific, and in summer and autumn the fish run upstream in huge numbers, followed by brown bears, eagles and fishermen, in about that order of seriousness.

The region's culture is a mix of Russian settlers, descended from Cossacks and later arrivals, and indigenous peoples, notably the Itelmen and Koryak, whose traditions of fishing and reindeer herding survive in some villages. In Milkovo, you will find a few shops, small cafes serving fish soup and dumplings, and basic accommodation.

Fill the tank here, buy food and water, and keep spare supplies for the road. Treat bears seriously, keep food sealed and do not wander off into the brush.
t.shashamane@7.2,38.6:
Shashamane sits on the main highway south from Addis Ababa, in the great Rift Valley, and it is exactly the sort of crossroads town that keeps a country moving. Trucks, minibuses, horse-drawn carts and motorbikes jostle in the streets, and the market sells everything from maize to mobile phones. About eighty-five thousand people live here, and the town has fuel stations, mechanics, cheap hotels and plenty of places to eat, making it a very practical place to begin a ride into the mountains. Hawassa, a larger lakeside city, is about twenty kilometres to the west.

What makes Shashamane special is a community that lives in one corner of it. In 1948, Emperor Haile Selassie granted land here to the Ethiopian World Federation, a Black American organisation, as a gift for people of African descent who wanted to return, and from the 1960s many Rastafarians from Jamaica and elsewhere settled in the area. Haile Selassie is revered in the Rastafari faith, and the community has kept its culture alive for generations, with music, colours of green, gold and red, and a strong sense of faith. Visitors are welcome in the community, if they come with respect.

The Rift Valley around the town is a land of lakes: Langano, a warm, brown lake popular for swimming, and the neighbouring Abijatta and Shalla, which lie in a national park full of flamingos and pelicans. Acacia trees, red earth and wide skies fill the landscape, and the air is warm. From Shashamane, a road branches east toward the Bale Mountains, climbing from the valley floor up to a cool, forested highland, a change that you notice in your lungs.

For the rider, this is a stop for supplies. Top up the tank, check the tyres, buy water and a snack, and ask about the state of the road ahead. Traffic is chaotic, with livestock, pedestrians and tuk-tuks all competing for space, and heavy trucks can be a real hazard. Avoid riding at night, when unlit vehicles and animals appear without warning. The dry season, from October to February, is the best time, while heavy rains from June to September can turn rough roads to mud.
t.harenna forest@6.7,39.7:
Harenna is the green southern face of the Bale Mountains, and getting there involves one of the most spectacular drops in Africa. The road crosses the Sanetti Plateau, a high, cold, open tableland at over 4,000 metres, studded with giant lobelias and small lakes, where Ethiopian wolves, among the rarest canids in the world, hunt for rodents in the grass. Then, at the edge of the plateau, the road plunges south through a series of bends into a forest, losing about a thousand five hundred metres in a few kilometres, and the air thickens, warms and fills with the smell of damp earth.

The Harenna Forest is among the largest remaining tracts of moist tropical forest in Ethiopia, a dense, mossy realm of ancient trees, tree ferns, bamboo and strangler figs, shrouded in mist. It is part of Bale Mountains National Park and a hotspot for biodiversity, with species found nowhere else, such as the Bale monkey, and it shelters leopards, giant forest hogs and black-maned lions, rarely seen. Wild Arabica coffee grows in the understory here, and Ethiopia is considered the original home of the plant.

The riding is hard. Much of the road is gravel, rough in places and slippery when it rains, which is often in the forest, and the descent from the plateau is steep and has sharp bends. The altitude and cold at the top can be a shock, with frost possible in the morning, and the contrast with the humid forest below is startling. Fog can obscure the road, so go slowly. This is a ride for someone with experience on rough tracks and a bike that can take them.

Services are almost non-existent, so carry fuel, water, food and a repair kit, and remember that mobile coverage is unreliable. The nearest reliable fuel is at Goba or Robe on the northern side, and it is worth filling every container you have before crossing. The park charges a fee at the gate, and rangers are helpful. Birdlife is exceptional, with Abyssinian catbirds and woodpeckers, and early morning is the time for the chorus. Visit between November and February, when the dry season gives the best chance of a passable road.
t.near marathon@24.7,-81.0:
Marathon is the middle of the Florida Keys, both geographically and in spirit, a town of about nine thousand people spread across a string of islands halfway between Key Largo and Key West. It is less polished than Islamorada and less wild than Key West, a working town of marinas, fishing boats, strip malls and seafood shacks, with the sea never more than a few hundred metres away on either side. The Overseas Highway runs straight through the middle, lined with businesses, and the mile markers, which count down from Key Largo to Key West, put Marathon at around mile 50.

The town owes its name, so the story goes, to the workers who built Henry Flagler's Overseas Railroad in the early twentieth century, who said that the work here was a marathon. The railroad, which reached Key West in 1912, was one of the great engineering feats of its time, but it was destroyed in 1935 by the Labor Day hurricane, one of the most powerful storms ever to hit the United States.
